Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette: Emma, a 78-year-old European American woman, has lived most of her life in a small suburban town with her husband. As a graphic designer, she spends much of her day surrounded by computers and print materials at an advertising firm where she has worked for decades. Emma's world changed dramatically when she experienced the traumatic impact of a devastating tornado that struck her community three months ago. The night of the tornado was one of sheer terror for Emma. She had been home alone, working on some late-night designs, when she heard a deafening roar outside. The sound grew louder until it felt like the world was about to come crashing down around her. The door to her office slammed open, and debris began flying through the air, shattering windows and tearing apart walls. Emma huddled in a closet for what seemed an eternity before help arrived. Since that night, Emma has found herself increasingly triggered by specific stimuli that remind her of the traumatic event. The sound of doors opening or slamming-whether it's at work when colleagues come into her office or even the creaking of doors in her home-can instantly catapult her back to the moment when the tornado ripped through her building. This has made her hyper-vigilant about any sudden movements and sounds, often leading her to jump up from her desk in alarm. Another trigger is the smell of alcohol, which oddly reminds Emma of the emergency responders who had used disinfectants and other chemicals during their rescue efforts. The scent of these substances can transport her back to that terrifying night, making it difficult for her to relax in social settings where alcoholic beverages are present. Emma has also found herself dwelling on how the event could have been prevented if only there had been better early warning systems or stronger building codes. This prevention rumination is a constant mental burden, as she repeatedly goes over scenarios and strategies that might have changed the outcome. In an effort to regain some sense of control in her life, Emma has taken up compulsive cleaning, often spending hours organizing and reorganizing her workspace and home. The memories of the tornado are fragmented and difficult for Emma to process. Sometimes she can recall what happened but feels completely numb, as if it had occurred to a stranger rather than herself. At other times, the memory feels so immediate that she is transported back to the terrifying experience, with every detail vividly present. The extreme nature of these memories makes them feel almost surreal and hard to believe. Emma's core beliefs about the world have been profoundly shaken by this event. She now holds a shattered view of how the world operates, seeing it as an unpredictable and dangerous place where terrible things can happen at any moment. This sense of injustice is particularly acute because she feels that nothing has been done to prevent such disasters from happening again or to help survivors like her. These negative appraisals have had a significant impact on Emma's daily life and relationships. Her husband, Tom, has noticed how much more tense and anxious Emma has become since the tornado. She often cancels plans with friends or avoids going out, preferring to stay home where she feels safer. At work, Emma's obsessive cleaning habits are beginning to affect her productivity, as she frequently gets distracted by organizing rather than focusing on design projects. Despite these difficulties, what finally brought Emma to seek help was the realization that she could not continue living in this constant state of anxiety and hypervigilance. She is most afraid of never being able to shake off the memories and triggers, but at the same time, she hopes for a future where she can regain some peace and control over her life. Emma believes that with support, she might be able to find a way to process her trauma and rebuild her sense of security in the world.
